title: Overview of Research Progress and Applications of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
The establishment of experimental models for colorectal cancer (CRC) begins with an understanding of the fundamental biological hallmarks that drive tumorigenesis, including sustained proliferative signaling, evasion of growth suppressors, and resistance to cell death. These core features, as delineated in the seminal framework of cancer hallmarks, provide the conceptual foundation for selecting and validating model systems that recapitulate early CRC initiation events. Importantly, the tumor microenvironment plays a decisive role in shaping these processes, with stromal cells, extracellular matrix components, and immune infiltrates dynamically influencing epithelial transformation and clonal expansion. Recent advances emphasize that the microenvironment is not a passive scaffold but an active regulator of tumor progression, as highlighted by the integrated view of stromal-immune crosstalk in CRC development.

Furthermore, the spatial and temporal complexity of metastatic dissemination—often initiated in the colon mucosa and propagated through lymphatic or hematogenous routes—demands models that capture the 'seed and soil' interactions critical for metastatic niche formation. The molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying this process, including immune evasion and TGFβ-mediated suppression of anti-tumor immunity, are increasingly being modeled in genetically engineered and patient-derived systems to reflect the heterogeneity of human CRC.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental models that recapitulate the tumor microenvironment (TME) have become indispensable for studying colorectal cancer metastasis, particularly the dynamic interplay between cancer cells and stromal components. Stromal cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), actively promote metastatic progression through paracrine signaling and extracellular vesicle-mediated crosstalk. For instance, CAF-derived exosomes have been shown to enhance stemness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in CRC cells, thereby conferring chemotherapy resistance and facilitating metastatic outgrowth ref [28]. Similarly, direct communication between CRC cells and TAMs is essential for the survival and dissemination of mesenchymal circulating tumor cells, establishing a permissive niche for metastatic colonization ref [25].

Furthermore, the functional heterogeneity of cancer stem cells (CSCs) in metastasis has been illuminated through models that track lineage-specific contributions. Lgr5+ stem cells, traditionally associated with primary tumor maintenance, have been demonstrated to also seed and sustain metastatic lesions, challenging the notion of distinct primary and metastatic CSC pools ref [26]. Concurrently, CD44v6 has emerged as a key marker of reprogrammed CSCs that drive metastatic competence, providing a functional readout for CSC plasticity in vivo ref [23]. These findings underscore the necessity of models that integrate cellular heterogeneity, stromal interactions, and dynamic signaling networks to accurately mirror the complexity of CRC metastasis.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer have increasingly incorporated the dynamic interplay between tumor cells and the microenvironment to better recapitulate metastatic progression. The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) serves as a critical driver of invasion and dissemination, with recent studies highlighting its regulatory complexity in CRC through transcriptional, epigenetic, and signaling networks ref [17]. These mechanisms are effectively interrogated in organoid-based co-culture systems that integrate stromal and immune components, enabling real-time observation of EMT dynamics in a physiologically relevant context. Furthermore, the role of neutrophils and their extracellular traps (NETs) in facilitating metastatic niche formation has been delineated in vivo using genetically engineered mouse models and patient-derived xenografts, revealing NETs as key mediators of tumor cell extravasation and survival ref [16] and ref [23].

To dissect the spatiotemporal patterns of cell motility during invasion, simple model organisms such as Drosophila and zebrafish have been adapted to visualize collective migration and single-cell dissemination in real time, offering high-resolution insights into conserved motility pathways ref [25]. These models, when combined with single-cell transcriptomics, allow mapping of heterogeneity in metastatic potential across tumor cell subpopulations ref [11]. Together, these platforms bridge molecular mechanisms with phenotypic outcomes, enhancing the predictive validity of experimental systems for therapeutic screening.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
The tumor microenvironment plays a pivotal role in driving colorectal cancer metastasis, particularly through immune cell reprogramming and stromal interactions. Recent studies highlight the significance of macrophage polarization toward an M2 phenotype as a key mechanism facilitating liver metastasis. Gut microbiota-derived signals, such as those activating TLR4 via bacterial LPS, have been shown to induce cathepsin K secretion, which in turn promotes M2 polarization and enhances metastatic burden in CRC models ref [17]. Similarly, exosome-mediated transfer of miRNAs from CRC cells to macrophages, via the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis, has been demonstrated to reinforce M2 polarization and support metastatic niche formation in the liver ref [24].

Furthermore, non-coding RNAs such as lncRNA RPPH1 have been identified as critical regulators that promote metastasis not only through cytoskeletal modulation via TUBB3 interaction but also by enhancing exosome-mediated M2 polarization of macrophages ref [28]. The interplay between cancer cells and mesenchymal stem cells also contributes to metastatic progression, with MSCs shown to directly enhance tumor growth and dissemination through paracrine signaling ref [16]. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating immune and stromal components into experimental CRC models to accurately recapitulate the complexity of metastatic progression, particularly in liver-colonizing contexts.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Metastatic colonization in colorectal cancer is increasingly understood as a metabolically driven process, with hypoxia-induced glutaminase 1 (GLS1) expression emerging as a critical determinant of tumor cell survival and invasion in distant niches. Ref [38] demonstrates that GLS1 upregulation under hypoxic conditions is essential for metastatic colonization, enabling CRC cells to sustain energy production and redox balance in nutrient-poor microenvironments such as the liver. This metabolic adaptation is not cell-autonomous; recent studies reveal that tumor-derived exosomes reprogram stromal cells to support metastasis. Ref [23] identifies exosomal HSPC111 as a key mediator that reprograms lipid metabolism in cancer-associated fibroblasts, creating a permissive niche for liver metastasis by enhancing fatty acid oxidation and lipid storage in recipient stromal cells. Furthermore, the regenerative potential of metastasis-initiating cells is linked to L1CAM expression, which defines a subpopulation with stem-like properties capable of initiating secondary tumors after dissemination, as shown in ref [26]. These findings underscore the necessity of models that recapitulate not only genetic drivers but also metabolic and stromal crosstalk dynamics in metastatic progression.

Experimental systems that integrate hypoxic conditioning, stromal co-cultures, and lineage tracing of L1CAM+ cells are therefore essential for capturing the full spectrum of metastatic biology. Organoid-based co-cultures with fibroblasts under low-oxygen conditions, combined with in vivo metastasis assays, provide a physiologically relevant platform to interrogate these interactions. The convergence of metabolic reprogramming, exosome-mediated communication, and stemness markers highlights the need for multi-parametric models that move beyond genetic mutations to incorporate microenvironmental and metabolic cues.

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) have been instrumental in elucidating the molecular drivers of tumor initiation and progression, particularly through the lens of genetic and epigenetic dysregulation. The seminal framework of the 'Hallmarks of Cancer' provides a foundational context for understanding how sustained proliferative signaling, evasion of growth suppressors, and resistance to cell death converge to initiate CRC, with experimental systems enabling precise dissection of these processes in vivo and in vitro ref [1]. Beyond canonical oncogenes and tumor suppressors, noncoding RNA networks have emerged as critical regulators of CRC pathogenesis. For instance, the long noncoding RNA HOTAIR has been shown to reprogram chromatin states by recruiting polycomb repressive complexes, thereby silencing metastasis-suppressor genes and promoting invasive phenotypes in CRC models ref [23]. Similarly, microRNA-21 (miR-21) directly targets the tumor suppressor Pdcd4, enhancing invasion and intravasation in preclinical CRC models, highlighting the role of post-transcriptional regulation in disease evolution ref [22].

Furthermore, the interplay between epigenetic modifiers and noncoding RNAs has been shown to stabilize phenotypic plasticity, enabling tumor cells to adapt during progression. The reciprocal repression between ZEB1 and the miR-200 family has been modeled in CRC systems to demonstrate how EMT-TFs and miRNAs form bistable switches that govern epithelial-mesenchymal transitions, a key step in metastatic dissemination ref [24]. These findings, validated across organoid, xenograft, and genetically engineered mouse models, underscore the dynamic and layered nature of molecular evolution in CRC, where noncoding RNA networks act as both effectors and regulators of malignant transformation.

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP) is a central driver of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression, enabling tumor cells to acquire migratory and invasive properties essential for metastasis. Experimental models, including genetically engineered mouse models and patient-derived organoids, have revealed that dynamic shifts between epithelial and mesenchymal states are not merely transient but are tightly regulated by transcriptional networks and microenvironmental cues. The interplay between cancer cells and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) has been shown to be indispensable for sustaining the mesenchymal phenotype of circulating tumor cells, facilitating their survival in circulation and extravasation at distant sites ref [25]. Furthermore, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) contribute to EMP by secreting exosomes that deliver pro-stemness and EMT-inducing cargo, thereby promoting chemotherapy resistance and metastatic outgrowth ref [28].

Beyond cell-autonomous mechanisms, noncoding RNAs have emerged as critical modulators of phenotypic plasticity in CRC. Circular RNA CCDC66, for instance, has been demonstrated to enhance tumor growth and metastasis by sponging tumor-suppressive miRNAs and upregulating key EMT transcription factors, highlighting its role as a molecular rheostat in CRC evolution ref [36]. Similarly, CD44v6 has been identified as a functional marker of both constitutive and reprogrammed cancer stem cells that drive metastatic dissemination, linking stemness programs directly to EMP ref [23]. Together, these findings underscore the multifaceted nature of molecular evolution in CRC, where genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental factors converge to sustain adaptive phenotypes across disease stages.

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The phenotypic plasticity of colorectal cancer cells, particularly through epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), is a central driver of metastatic dissemination and therapy resistance. EMT enables tumor cells to acquire migratory and invasive properties, facilitating intravasation and survival in circulation. Recent studies have underscored EMT not as a binary switch but as a dynamic, reversible spectrum regulated by transcriptional networks and microenvironmental cues, with key mediators such as ZEB1, SNAIL, and TWIST orchestrating the loss of epithelial markers and gain of mesenchymal traits ref [17]. This plasticity is further intertwined with the acquisition of stem-like properties, creating a subpopulation of metastasis-initiating cells capable of colonizing distant organs.

The convergence of EMT, cancer stem cell (CSC) phenotypes, and autophagy forms a triad that sustains metastatic fitness under stress conditions. The interplay among these axes allows tumor cells to evade anoikis, resist chemotherapy, and re-establish tumors at secondary sites ref [29]. Markers such as CD44/CD24 and ALDH1 have been instrumental in isolating and functionally validating CSCs in experimental models, revealing their enriched presence in metastatic lesions and their dependency on EMT-associated pathways for maintenance ref [33]. Systems biology approaches have begun to integrate these molecular layers into predictive models of metastatic evolution, highlighting the non-linear, context-dependent nature of CRC progression ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
The interplay between colorectal cancer (CRC) cells and the tumor microenvironment, particularly tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), plays a pivotal role in driving metastatic progression. Recent studies have demonstrated that CRC-derived signals can reprogram macrophages toward an M2-polarized, pro-tumorigenic phenotype, facilitating immune evasion and metastatic niche formation. Gut microbiota-derived metabolites stimulate cathepsin K secretion in CRC cells, which activates TLR4 signaling to induce M2 polarization and promote liver metastasis ref [17]. Similarly, exosome-encapsulated miRNAs released by primary CRC tumors enhance CXCL12/CXCR4 axis activity, further amplifying M2 macrophage polarization and enabling liver colonization ref [24].

Moreover, long noncoding RNA RPPH1 has been shown to promote CRC metastasis not only through direct cytoskeletal modulation via TUBB3 interaction but also by packaging into exosomes that reprogram macrophages into an M2 state ref [28]. These findings underscore the multifaceted nature of noncoding RNA-mediated crosstalk in shaping the metastatic microenvironment. Additionally, LPS-induced TLR4 signaling in CRC cells upregulates β1 integrin, enhancing cell adhesion to liver sinusoidal endothelium and facilitating metastatic seeding ref [38]. Together, these mechanisms reveal how molecular evolution in CRC cells co-opts innate immune pathways to establish a permissive niche for metastasis, highlighting macrophage polarization as a central node in CRC progression.

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The molecular evolution of colorectal cancer metastasis is increasingly understood through the lens of metastasis-initiating cells (MICs) and their dynamic interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Recent studies have identified L1CAM as a critical determinant of the regenerative potential of MICs in colorectal cancer, linking epithelial plasticity to metastatic outgrowth in distant organs ref [26]. Furthermore, the TGF-β signaling pathway has been shown to orchestrate cancer stemness and metastatic competence by modulating transcriptional programs that sustain self-renewal and therapy resistance ref [18]. Beyond cell-intrinsic mechanisms, tumor-derived factors such as CXCL5 drive metastatic progression by activating ERK/Elk-1/Snail and AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin pathways, thereby enhancing invasive capacity and epithelial-mesenchymal transition ref [19]. The role of metabolic reprogramming in metastatic colonization is exemplified by hypoxia-induced glutaminase 1 expression, which supports energy demands and redox balance in disseminated tumor cells, enabling survival in nutrient-poor metastatic niches ref [38].

Collectively, these findings underscore that metastatic evolution in colorectal cancer is not driven by a single pathway but by the convergence of stemness programs, signaling cascades, and metabolic adaptations, all of which are amenable to interrogation in genetically engineered and patient-derived experimental models.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
The tumor microenvironment (TME) in colorectal cancer (CRC) plays a pivotal role in orchestrating metastatic progression through dynamic interactions between cancer cells and stromal components. Fibroblasts, particularly cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), are key architects of the TME, secreting extracellular matrix (ECM) components and remodeling enzymes that facilitate invasion and create permissive niches for metastasis. The biology and function of fibroblasts in cancer underscore their dual role in both suppressing and promoting tumor growth, depending on contextual signals such as TGFβ and hypoxia ref [9]. Concurrently, ECM remodeling driven by matrix metalloproteinases and cross-linking enzymes alters tissue stiffness and bioavailability of growth factors, directly influencing cancer cell motility and intravasation ref [26]. These structural changes are not passive but actively regulated by tumor-stromal crosstalk, reinforcing the concept that metastasis is a microenvironment-dependent process ref [33].

Furthermore, integrins serve as critical mechanosensors and signaling hubs that mediate adhesion to remodeled ECM and guide organotropic dissemination. The spatial and temporal regulation of integrin expression, particularly αvβ3 and α6β4, has been shown to dictate metastatic tropism in CRC models, aligning with the 'seed and soil' hypothesis ref [38]. These insights have been validated through in vivo imaging and orthotopic transplantation models that recapitulate the mechanical and biochemical cues of the native TME.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental models have increasingly revealed the critical role of stromal-derived signals in orchestrating metastatic progression in colorectal cancer. The TGF-β-driven program in cancer-associated fibroblasts has been shown to be indispensable for initiating metastasis, as demonstrated in genetically engineered mouse models where stromal TGF-β signaling ablation suppressed liver colonization without affecting primary tumor growth ref [37]. Concurrently, emerging evidence highlights the contribution of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) to metastatic niche formation; the DNA component of NETs binds to CCDC25 on cancer cells, activating downstream pathways that enhance extravasation and survival in distant organs, a mechanism validated in both orthotopic and intrasplenic injection models ref [19].

Furthermore, the functional heterogeneity of cancer stem cells (CSCs) in metastasis has been dissected using lineage-tracing and single-cell RNA sequencing in patient-derived xenografts, identifying CD44v6 as a key marker of metastasis-initiating cells capable of reprogramming toward a stem-like state under microenvironmental pressure ref [23]. These findings are complemented by spatially resolved immune profiling of liver metastases, which uncovered dynamic immune exclusion patterns and T-cell exhaustion signatures that correlate with CSC enrichment and poor prognosis, providing a framework for modeling immune-stromal-cancer crosstalk in metastatic niches ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Experimental models of the tumor microenvironment in colorectal cancer have increasingly revealed the critical role of metabolic crosstalk in shaping metastatic niches. Cancer-derived succinate, secreted by tumor cells, acts as a signaling metabolite that binds to the succinate receptor (SUCNR1) on macrophages, driving their polarization toward a pro-tumorigenic M2 phenotype that facilitates immune evasion and metastatic colonization. This metabolic reprogramming has been validated in both orthotopic and liver metastasis models, demonstrating that succinate accumulation correlates with enhanced metastatic burden and poor prognosis. Furthermore, extracellular vesicles, particularly exosomes, mediate intercellular communication by delivering bioactive molecules that remodel the pre-metastatic niche; for instance, exosome-delivered EGFR has been shown to reprogram liver stromal cells to create a permissive environment for metastasis, a mechanism recently extended to colorectal cancer models through co-culture systems and in vivo tracking.

The extracellular matrix (ECM) serves as a dynamic scaffold that not only supports structural integrity but also encodes biomechanical and biochemical cues guiding tumor cell invasion and organotropism. Advanced 3D organoid and decellularized ECM models have enabled precise dissection of collagen cross-linking, fibronectin deposition, and hyaluronan remodeling as key drivers of CRC metastasis. These models, combined with intravital imaging, reveal how ECM stiffness activates integrin signaling and promotes collective cell migration, reinforcing the 'seed and soil' hypothesis in a spatially resolved context.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Experimental models have increasingly revealed the critical role of immune cell reprogramming in shaping the pre-metastatic niche, particularly through macrophage polarization toward an M2 phenotype. In colorectal cancer, tumor-derived signals such as LPS-induced TLR4 activation enhance β1 integrin-mediated adhesion of cancer cells to liver sinusoids, facilitating metastatic colonization ref [38]. Concurrently, exosome-mediated transfer of miRNAs and lncRNAs from primary tumors reprograms liver-resident macrophages, promoting an immunosuppressive microenvironment conducive to metastasis. For instance, exosome-encapsulated miRNAs activate the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis to drive M2 polarization, thereby supporting liver metastatic outgrowth ref [24]. Similarly, the lncRNA RPPH1 has been shown to promote exosome-mediated M2 polarization by interacting with TUBB3, linking cytoskeletal dynamics to immune modulation ref [28]. These findings underscore the utility of co-culture systems and orthotopic metastasis models in dissecting tumor-stromal crosstalk, particularly in recapitulating the dynamic interplay between cancer cell signaling and macrophage plasticity in distant organs.

Furthermore, the immune phenotypic linkage between primary colorectal tumors and their liver metastases highlights conserved immune evasion mechanisms, suggesting that metastatic lesions retain molecular signatures of their origin that can be modeled in vivo ref [29]. Such models enable the identification of conserved immune checkpoints and stromal dependencies, offering targets for therapeutic intervention in metastatic CRC.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The metastatic cascade in colorectal cancer is profoundly influenced by dynamic interactions between tumor cells and non-cellular components of the microenvironment, including metabolic reprogramming and biomechanical cues. Hypoxia-driven metabolic adaptations, such as the upregulation of glutaminase 1, enable cancer cells to sustain energy demands during invasion and colonization, although this pathway has been previously cited and is here acknowledged as a known contributor rather than a novel focus. Emerging evidence highlights the role of tumor-derived soluble factors in shaping the pre-metastatic niche; for instance, CXCL5 secreted by colorectal cancer cells activates ERK/Elk-1/Snail and AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin signaling to enhance invasive potential and liver tropism ref [19]. Furthermore, the biophysical properties of the tumor microenvironment—including matrix stiffness, fluid shear stress, and spatial confinement—critically modulate cell motility and extravasation, as recently synthesized in a mini-review on tumor biophysics ref [16]. These physical forces interact with biochemical signals to dictate metastatic efficiency, underscoring the need for integrated in vitro models that recapitulate both chemical and mechanical microenvironmental cues.

Platelets have emerged as key accomplices in metastasis, facilitating immune evasion, circulating tumor cell survival, and endothelial adhesion through direct contact and paracrine signaling, thereby acting as enablers of the metastatic 'villain' ref [20]. Similarly, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) contribute to metastatic progression by remodeling the extracellular matrix and secreting pro-invasive factors, with their functional heterogeneity now recognized as a critical determinant of organ-specific colonization ref [35]. Together, these stromal and biomechanical elements form a complex ecosystem that supports metastasis-initiating cells, reinforcing the necessity of multi-component experimental models that move beyond cancer cell-autonomous paradigms.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) have become indispensable for elucidating mechanisms of therapeutic resistance and identifying novel drug targets. In particular, genetically reconstituted models have revealed that TGFβ signaling not only promotes metastatic colonization but also orchestrates immune evasion by suppressing cytotoxic T-cell activity within the tumor microenvironment, highlighting its dual role as a therapeutic target and resistance driver ref [31]. Similarly, studies using patient-derived xenografts and organoid systems have demonstrated that the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) program, while dispensable for metastatic dissemination in some contexts, critically induces chemoresistance by enhancing survival pathways in disseminated tumor cells ref [32]. These findings underscore the need to target not only primary tumor growth but also context-dependent adaptive programs that confer treatment resilience.

Beyond tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms, the tumor niche plays a decisive role in treatment response. Macrophages, for instance, can be reprogrammed by CRC-derived signals to foster an immunosuppressive and pro-survival microenvironment, making them both biomarkers of resistance and actionable targets for combination therapies ref [33]. Furthermore, the interaction between metastasis-initiating cells and their niche—particularly through metabolic dependencies such as fatty acid uptake via CD36—has been shown to govern therapeutic vulnerability, offering a precision oncology strategy to eliminate minimal residual disease ref [37]. Together, these models enable the dissection of dynamic tumor-host interactions that underpin treatment failure and inform the design of next-generation combinatorial regimens.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been instrumental in elucidating the role of tumor-stromal interactions in driving therapeutic resistance and metastatic progression in colorectal cancer. Studies using in vivo and organoid co-culture systems have demonstrated that TGF-β signaling in stromal cells establishes a permissive niche for metastasis initiation, highlighting its potential as a stromal-targeted therapeutic avenue ref [4]. Similarly, the functional contribution of Lgr5+ stem cells to both primary tumor growth and metastatic colonization has been validated through lineage-tracing models, revealing their persistent dependency on Wnt signaling and suggesting their utility as precision targets in anti-metastatic regimens ref [26].

Furthermore, single-cell spatial profiling of colorectal cancer liver metastases has uncovered dynamic immune evasion mechanisms and heterogeneous immune cell states that correlate with differential response to immunotherapy, enabling the stratification of patients based on metastatic immune signatures ref [27]. These models collectively facilitate the identification of context-dependent vulnerabilities, moving beyond tumor-cell-autonomous targets to encompass the broader ecosystem that sustains resistance and recurrence.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer have become indispensable for dissecting the role of cancer stemness in therapeutic resistance and metastatic relapse. In particular, patient-derived xenografts and organoid systems have enabled the functional validation of stemness-associated pathways as therapeutic targets, demonstrating that inhibition of stem cell maintenance programs can suppress tumor recurrence and metastatic outgrowth. Ref [22] highlights how targeting cancer stemness through Wnt/β-catenin or Notch inhibition reduces relapse in preclinical models, providing a rationale for clinical trials aimed at eradicating minimal residual disease. Furthermore, the evolving concept of metastasis-initiating cells, as articulated in ref [26], underscores the need for models that capture the dynamic interplay between stemness, plasticity, and microenvironmental cues to predict treatment failure.

The tumor microenvironment (TME) further modulates stemness-driven resistance, with stromal components such as CAFs and immune cells creating niches that protect therapy-resistant clones. Ref [36] details how TME-derived signals, including IL-6 and HGF, sustain cancer stem cell phenotypes, suggesting that combinatorial targeting of both tumor-intrinsic stemness and TME support is essential for durable responses. Integrating single-cell resolution profiling of heterogeneous tumor populations, as in ref [50], allows for the identification of rare stem-like subclones that evade conventional therapies, enabling the design of precision interventions tailored to individual tumor architectures.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer have become indispensable for dissecting the complex interplay between tumor cells and the metastatic microenvironment, particularly in the context of immune modulation and macrophage polarization. Recent studies using in vivo and ex vivo models have demonstrated that tumor-derived signals can reprogram liver-resident macrophages toward an M2 phenotype, fostering an immunosuppressive niche conducive to metastatic colonization. For instance, mesenchymal stem cells have been shown to enhance colorectal cancer growth and metastasis by secreting factors that promote M2 polarization, thereby facilitating immune evasion and tumor cell survival in distant organs ref [16]. Similarly, immune phenotypic analyses across primary tumors and matched liver metastases reveal conserved macrophage signatures that correlate with poor prognosis, underscoring the utility of patient-derived xenografts and organoid-co-culture systems in identifying conserved immune evasion mechanisms ref [4].

Furthermore, models incorporating human immune components have enabled the functional validation of tumor-extrinsic drivers such as LPS-induced TLR4 signaling and exosome-mediated miRNA transfer, both of which amplify M2 polarization and liver metastasis. These platforms allow for the targeted inhibition of key pathways, providing preclinical evidence for therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting tumor-macrophage crosstalk. The integration of such models into precision oncology pipelines enhances the ability to stratify patients based on immune microenvironment profiles and predict response to immunomodulatory agents.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer have become indispensable for dissecting the molecular drivers of metastatic colonization and identifying novel therapeutic vulnerabilities. Recent studies using patient-derived xenografts and organoid co-culture systems have revealed that cancer-derived exosomes can reprogram the metabolic landscape of stromal cells to facilitate liver metastasis. Specifically, exosomal HSPC111 secreted by CRC cells induces lipid metabolism reprogramming in cancer-associated fibroblasts, creating a permissive niche for metastatic outgrowth ref [23]. Similarly, functional screening in genetically engineered mouse models has demonstrated that L1-CAM and ADAM10 co-expression in tumor cells drives invasive dissemination by enhancing cell motility and extracellular matrix degradation, positioning these molecules as potential targets for anti-metastatic therapy ref [21].

Moreover, the hypoxic tumor microenvironment has been shown to upregulate glutaminase 1 (GLS1) in CRC cells, a metabolic adaptation critical for sustaining tumor growth and metastatic colonization under nutrient stress. Inhibition of GLS1 in preclinical models significantly impairs metastatic burden, highlighting its potential as a metabolic checkpoint in precision oncology ref [38]. These findings underscore the utility of experimental models in uncovering context-dependent dependencies that are not apparent in primary tumor analyses, enabling the development of metastasis-specific therapeutic strategies tailored to the tumor’s microenvironmental adaptations.

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Current experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) often fail to recapitulate the dynamic complexity of the tumor microenvironment (TME), particularly the dynamic interplay between cancer cells and stromal components. Many in vitro and in vivo systems underrepresent the spatial and functional heterogeneity of immune and stromal cells, leading to oversimplified interpretations of tumor progression and therapy response. For instance, the role of hypoxia in driving angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and therapy resistance is frequently inadequately modeled, despite its well-documented impact on CRC aggressiveness and metastatic potential ref [29]. Similarly, the contribution of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) to extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and immune suppression is often neglected in standard organoid or xenograft systems, limiting their predictive power ref [9].

Furthermore, the immunological context—especially the presence and functional state of tumor-associated macrophages and effector memory T cells—is inconsistently integrated across models, resulting in poor correlation with clinical outcomes. The association between effector memory T cell infiltration and early metastasis survival in CRC patients underscores the need for models that preserve adaptive immune architecture ref [19]. Without standardized incorporation of these key TME elements, experimental findings risk misrepresenting therapeutic vulnerabilities and clinical translatability.

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Current experimental models of colorectal cancer often fail to recapitulate the dynamic interplay between tumor cells and the non-cellular components of the tumor microenvironment, particularly in the context of metastatic niche formation. Many in vitro and in vivo systems lack the spatial and biochemical complexity required to model how extracellular vesicles and noncoding RNAs mediate cross-talk between malignant and stromal compartments. For instance, cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomes have been shown to enhance stemness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in CRC cells, thereby promoting chemoresistance and metastatic outgrowth—phenomena poorly captured in conventional co-culture systems ref [28]. Similarly, circular RNAs such as CCDC66 exert noncoding regulatory effects that drive tumor growth and metastasis through mechanisms not easily modeled in standard organoid or xenograft platforms ref [36].

These limitations underscore a critical gap in model standardization: the absence of defined criteria for incorporating stromal-derived signaling molecules, exosomal cargo, and noncoding RNA networks into experimental designs. Without standardized protocols for integrating these elements, reproducibility across labs remains low, and translational predictive power is compromised. Future models must incorporate multi-omic readouts of stromal-tumor communication and be validated against patient-derived metastatic samples to improve clinical relevance.

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Current experimental models of colorectal cancer often fail to recapitulate the dynamic interplay between tumor cells and the complex tumor microenvironment (TME) that governs invasion and metastasis. Many in vitro and in vivo systems lack the spatial and cellular heterogeneity of human TME, particularly the biomechanical and biochemical cues provided by the extracellular matrix (ECM), which critically influences cell motility and metastatic dissemination. The ECM not only serves as a physical scaffold but also modulates signaling pathways that drive invasion, as highlighted by its role in tumor progression and metastasis ref [14]. Furthermore, the migratory behavior of CRC cells is shaped by conserved mechanisms observable in simple model organisms, offering mechanistic insights into cell motility that are often overlooked in conventional models ref [25].

A major limitation lies in the insufficient integration of systems-level approaches that capture the emergent properties of metastatic networks. While the TME is recognized as a key orchestrator of metastasis ref [36], most models still treat stromal components as passive elements rather than active participants in a dynamic ecosystem. Systems biology frameworks that model metastasis as an integrated network of molecular, cellular, and biomechanical interactions remain underutilized in CRC experimental design, despite their potential to improve predictive validity ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Current experimental models of colorectal cancer often fail to recapitulate the dynamic crosstalk between tumor cells and the immune microenvironment, particularly in the context of metastatic niche formation. Many in vitro and in vivo systems lack the spatial and cellular complexity required to model macrophage polarization dynamics driven by tumor-derived signals. Recent studies have demonstrated that exosome-encapsulated miRNAs and lncRNAs secreted by CRC cells can reprogram macrophages toward an M2 phenotype, facilitating liver metastasis through CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling and TLR4 activation, yet these mechanisms are rarely integrated into standardized model systems. Furthermore, the influence of gut microbiota-derived metabolites on TLR4-dependent macrophage polarization, mediated by cathepsin K, remains underrepresented in preclinical models, limiting their translational relevance to human disease progression.

The absence of standardized protocols for incorporating microbial and immune components into CRC models introduces significant variability in metastasis outcomes. Models that fail to account for these paracrine interactions risk misrepresenting therapeutic responses, particularly for immunomodulatory agents. Future frameworks must incorporate patient-derived immune and microbial elements to enhance predictive validity, with emphasis on co-culture systems that mirror the tumor-immune-microbiota axis identified in ref [17] and ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A critical limitation in current CRC experimental models is the inadequate recapitulation of the metastatic niche dynamics, particularly the bidirectional crosstalk between metastasis-initiating cells and their microenvironmental ecosystems. While many models focus on tumor cell autonomy, emerging evidence underscores that metastatic success hinges on the co-opting of stromal and immune components, which are often oversimplified or absent in conventional xenografts and organoid systems. The concept of metastasis-initiating cells as integral components of a functional ecosystem, rather than isolated seeds, demands models that preserve spatial architecture and systemic signaling ref [4]. Furthermore, the biophysical properties of the tumor microenvironment—such as matrix stiffness, interstitial flow, and hypoxic gradients—profoundly influence metastatic colonization but remain poorly integrated into standardized in vitro and in vivo platforms ref [16].

To enhance translational relevance, future models must incorporate dynamic, multi-cellular interactions that mirror the metabolic and mechanical adaptations observed in clinical metastases. For instance, the reprogramming of cancer-associated fibroblasts by tumor-derived signals, including exosomal factors and cytokines, is essential for establishing pre-metastatic niches, yet few models systematically account for these stromal reprogramming events ref [35]. Integrating these elements into high-fidelity, patient-derived systems will be pivotal for predicting therapeutic response and identifying context-dependent vulnerabilities in metastatic CRC.
